extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and scientifically literate general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence Darwin uses to argue that complex instincts and social structures (e.g., slave-making ants, hive-bee comb-building, sterile castes) can be explained by natural selection acting on slight, successive modifications of simpler instincts. Emphasises comparative, experimental, mechanistic, and selective-pressure arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage to the species without exterminating the exploited species
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection can make an occasional habit permanent, if of advantage to the species, and if the insect whose nest and stored food are thus feloniously appropriated, be not thus exterminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed adaptive habit (e.g., parasitism or slave-making) must confer a net advantage to the species adopting it while not eliminating the host/prey species; Darwin uses this as a condition under which occasional opportunistic behaviour could be fixed by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observation and experimental demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and simple experiments (e.g., opening nests, introducing a single slave F. fusca which immediately performs work) used to establish the facts of slave-making and dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims about instincts are supported by direct field observations and manipulations (e.g., watching migrations, introducing individuals). Reproducible, well-documented natural-history observations and small interventions that change behaviour are required to substantiate hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional role identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what functions different members perform (e.g., slaves tend larvæ and search for aphides; masters perform raids and carry slaves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain adaptive value by identifying the roles that behavioural types perform within the community; distinguish who builds, who tends brood, who forages, and how that division affects community success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual, stepwise adaptive explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each profitable modification must be slight and profitable to the individual under its conditions of life; natural selection acts by the accumulation of slight modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex instincts must be shown to be reachable by a long, graduated succession of useful intermediate states. One should propose plausible intermediate stages and explain how each stage increases fitness (Darwin repeatedly stresses gradual, useful modifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative evidence across related species (gradation principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graded series of species (e.g., humble-bees → Melipona → hive-bee) to show intermediate forms and structural progression toward complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare closely related taxa to demonstrate intermediate structural or behavioural forms that bridge simple and complex states; such comparative gradations support gradual evolution by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of plausible selective pressure linked to fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy of wax (and thereby economy of honey) is invoked as the motive power of selection favoring more economical comb construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain which resource or fitness component is being economised or enhanced (here: wax/honey economy) and argue quantitatively or qualitatively that small savings confer competitive advantage to colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic decomposition into simple component instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex structures (like hexagonal combs) can result from a few very simple instincts (e.g., bees sweeping equal spheres at given distances and building walls at planes of intersection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a proximate-mechanistic account showing how simple, observable behaviours combine to produce the complex outcome, demonstrating plausibility without invoking foresight or design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental testability of the mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory can be tested by experiments (e.g., placing strips/ridges of wax and observing bee excavation and building behaviour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory explanation should suggest and withstand simple, falsifiable experiments that replicate or challenge the proposed mechanism; Darwin gives concrete experimental manipulations and expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of intermediate or transitional states in populations
rubrics_metrics.description: If gradual selection produced complex castes or structures, we ought occasionally to find neuter-insects in the same nest presenting gradations of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for within-species or within-nest variation that shows intermediate morphologies/behaviours; such findings support cumulative selection rather than sudden origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritability of advantageous modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The modifications that are selected must be transmitted to offspring (Darwin repeatedly assumes inheritance of slight profitable modifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue or demonstrate that the behavioural/structural variations have a heritable basis such that parents producing advantageous variants leave more successful descendants; Darwin invokes inheritance as a necessary condition for cumulative selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for multilevel selection (family/community selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection may be applied to the family as well as to the individual; family-selection can explain the origin of sterile castes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When individual sterility prevents direct transmission, consider selection acting at the family or colony level — i.e., fertile parents that produce useful sterile offspring may be favoured — and show how this can accumulate modifications correlated with sterility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of traits with sex, age, or sterile condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters can become correlated with sex, age, or sterility (as with nuptial plumage or differential horns), enabling caste differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known analogies (sexual dimorphism, age-limited traits) to justify how traits could become linked to the sterile condition and thus be shaped by selection acting on breeding individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for coordinated collective construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how many individuals working together (each shifting between cells) nonetheless produce coherent structures (balance struck between workers standing at relative distances and excavating/building equally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a model of social coordination (simple rules like equal spacing and circular excavation) that explains how uncoordinated individual actions yield precise collective architecture; cite experimental or observational evidence (e.g., vermilion wax marking).
